title: Problem Overview: Almost Additive Functions
content:
**Erdős Problem #1126: Almost Additive Functions**

If $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$ for almost all pairs $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, can $f$ be 'repaired' to satisfy the equation for ALL pairs?

**Answer: YES** — proved by de Bruijn (1966) and Jurkat (1965) independently.

The repaired function $g$ agrees with $f$ almost everywhere and is unique among additive functions. This is a stability theorem for Cauchy's equation: approximate solutions (in the measure-theoretic sense) are near exact solutions.
mathContext: The theorem states: $\text{IsAlmostAdditive}(f) \Rightarrow \exists g,\, \text{IsAdditive}(g) \wedge f =_{\text{a.e.}} g$. It connects Cauchy's functional equation with Lebesgue measure theory and fits into the Hyers-Ulam stability framework.

title: Imports and Setup
content: Imports `Mathlib.Data.Real.Basic` for $\mathbb{R}$, `Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Measure.Lebesgue.Basic` for Lebesgue measure, and `Mathlib.Topology.Basic` for continuity. Opens the `MeasureTheory` namespace for direct access to `volume` (Lebesgue measure).
mathContext: The formalization works with Lebesgue measure $\lambda$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}^2$ via `MeasureTheory.volume`. The product measure on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is used for `ae_pairs`.

title: IsAdditive: Cauchy's Functional Equation
content:
**Definition**: `IsAdditive f` iff $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Cauchy (1821) studied this equation and showed that continuous solutions must be linear: $f(x) = cx$. The simplest examples are $f = \text{id}$ and $f(x) = cx$. Without continuity, Hamel (1905) showed that wild (non-measurable, everywhere discontinuous) solutions exist using the Axiom of Choice.

Additive functions are exactly the $\mathbb{Q}$-linear maps $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$. Choosing values freely on a Hamel basis (a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis for $\mathbb{R}$) gives any $\mathbb{Q}$-linear function.
mathContext: The set of additive functions $\text{Hom}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R})$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space of dimension $|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{\aleph_0}$. Only a 1-dimensional subspace consists of continuous (linear) functions.

title: Identity is Additive
content:
**Theorem** (`id_is_additive`): The identity function $f(x) = x$ satisfies $f(x+y) = x + y = f(x) + f(y)$.

Proved by `simp [id]`. This is the simplest non-zero additive function, corresponding to $c = 1$ in $f(x) = cx$.
mathContext: The identity $\text{id}: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is both $\mathbb{Q}$-linear and $\mathbb{R}$-linear. It generates the continuous additive functions under scalar multiplication.

title: Scalar Multiples are Additive
content:
**Theorem** (`scalar_is_additive`): For any $c \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = cx$ is additive: $c(x+y) = cx + cy$.

Proved by `ring`. These are all the continuous additive functions (Cauchy's theorem). The proof that no others exist requires continuity or some regularity condition.
mathContext: The map $c \mapsto (x \mapsto cx)$ embeds $\mathbb{R}$ into $\text{Hom}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R})$. Its image is exactly the continuous additive functions.

title: Continuous Additive Functions are Linear
content:
**Axiom** (`continuous_additive_is_linear`): If $f$ is additive and continuous, then $f(x) = cx$ for some $c \in \mathbb{R}$.

This is Cauchy's classical theorem (1821). The proof: additivity gives $f(q) = qf(1)$ for $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ by induction. Continuity extends to $f(x) = xf(1)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ by density of $\mathbb{Q}$. So $c = f(1)$.

Axiomatized because the full proof requires careful handling of rational approximation in Lean.
mathContext: Cauchy's theorem: $f \in C(\mathbb{R}) \cap \text{Hom}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R}) \Rightarrow f(x) = f(1) \cdot x$. The key step is $f(q) = q \cdot f(1)$ for $q \in \mathbb{Q}$, then continuity + density of $\mathbb{Q}$.

title: ae_holds: Almost Everywhere (1D)
content:
**Definition**: `ae_holds P` iff there exists a null set $N \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ with $\lambda(N) = 0$ such that $P(x)$ holds for all $x \notin N$.

This is a pedagogical version of Mathlib's `∀ᵐ x ∂μ, P x` using `Filter.Eventually`. The explicit null set makes the definition more transparent for this problem.
mathContext: In Mathlib, `∀ᵐ x ∂μ, P x` means $P$ holds $\mu$-a.e. This definition is equivalent when $\mu$ is Lebesgue measure. The explicit $N$ makes Fubini-type arguments more visible.

title: ae_pairs: Almost All Pairs (2D)
content:
**Definition**: `ae_pairs P` iff there exists a null set $N \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with $\lambda_2(N) = 0$ such that $P(x,y)$ holds for all $(x,y) \notin N$.

The 2D measure here is the product Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^2$. By Fubini's theorem, $\lambda_2(N) = 0$ implies that for a.e. $x$, the section $\{y : (x,y) \in N\}$ has 1D measure zero. This Fubini connection is central to the de Bruijn-Jurkat proof.
mathContext: Fubini's theorem: $\lambda_2(N) = 0 \iff$ for $\lambda$-a.e. $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the section $N_x = \{y : (x,y) \in N\}$ satisfies $\lambda(N_x) = 0$. This relates 2D null sets to 1D null sets.

title: IsAlmostAdditive: The Central Definition
content:
**Definition**: `IsAlmostAdditive f` iff $f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y)$ for almost all $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$.

This is `ae_pairs (fun x y => f (x + y) = f x + f y)`. The exceptional set where additivity fails has 2D Lebesgue measure zero. Note that this is much weaker than pointwise additivity: the exceptional set can be uncountable (just measure zero).

Every truly additive function is almost additive (take $N = \emptyset$). The theorem says the converse holds up to a.e. modification.
mathContext: The space of almost-additive functions modulo a.e. equivalence is isomorphic to the space of additive functions. This is the content of the de Bruijn-Jurkat theorem plus uniqueness.

title: ae_eq: Almost Everywhere Equality
content:
**Definition**: `ae_eq f g` iff $f(x) = g(x)$ for almost all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

This defines an equivalence relation on functions $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$. Two functions are a.e. equal if they differ only on a null set. This is the standard identification used in $L^p$ spaces.
mathContext: The quotient $L^0(\mathbb{R}) = \{\text{measurable } f\}/\sim_{\text{a.e.}}$ identifies functions differing on null sets. The de Bruijn-Jurkat theorem works in this quotient.

title: de Bruijn-Jurkat Theorem (Main Result)
content:
**Axiom** (`de_bruijn_jurkat_theorem`): If $f$ is almost additive, there exists a truly additive $g$ with $f = g$ a.e.

**Proof sketch** (not formalized): For a.e. $x$, define $g(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} f(nx)/n$. By almost-additivity, $f(nx) \approx nf(x)$ for a.e. $x$, so the limit exists a.e. One shows $g$ is additive everywhere (using Fubini to handle the null sets) and $g = f$ a.e.

The key difficulty is showing $g$ is additive for ALL pairs, not just a.e. pairs. This requires careful Fubini arguments: for each fixed $x$, additivity holds for a.e. $y$; then for each fixed $y$, it holds for a.e. $x$; iterating pins down the value everywhere.

Wrapped as `erdos_1126_main` for clarity.
mathContext: The construction $g(x) = \lim_{n} f(nx)/n$ uses the ergodic-theoretic idea that $f(nx)/n \to g(x)$ by the 'law of large numbers' for the additive cocycle $f$. Alternatively, one can use Steinhaus's theorem: if $A$ has positive measure, then $A - A$ contains an interval.

title: Uniqueness: Additive + a.e. Equal implies Equal
content:
**Axiom** (`additive_ae_unique`): If $g_1$ and $g_2$ are both additive and $g_1 = g_2$ a.e., then $g_1 = g_2$ everywhere.

The proof reduces to showing that an additive function zero a.e. is identically zero. If $g = g_1 - g_2$ is additive and zero a.e., then $\{x : g(x) = 0\}$ has full measure. Since this set is a subgroup of $(\mathbb{R}, +)$, and a measurable subgroup of positive measure must be all of $\mathbb{R}$ (by Steinhaus), $g = 0$.
mathContext: Steinhaus's theorem: if $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is measurable with $\lambda(A) > 0$, then $A - A$ contains an open interval around 0. Applied to $A = g^{-1}(0)$: since $A$ is an additive subgroup with $\lambda(A) > 0$, $A - A = A$ contains an interval, so $A$ is dense and closed (as kernel of additive $g$), hence $A = \mathbb{R}$.

title: Additive and Zero a.e. implies Zero
content:
**Axiom** (`additive_zero_ae`): If $g$ is additive and $g = 0$ a.e., then $g = 0$ identically.

This is the key lemma for uniqueness. The set $\{x : g(x) = 0\} = \ker(g)$ is an additive subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$. If it has positive measure (in fact, full measure since $g = 0$ a.e.), Steinhaus's theorem forces it to contain an interval, making the subgroup dense and closed, hence all of $\mathbb{R}$.
mathContext: An additive subgroup $H \leq (\mathbb{R}, +)$ with $\lambda(H) > 0$ must equal $\mathbb{R}$. Proof: by Steinhaus, $H - H \supseteq (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $H$ is a subgroup, $H - H = H$, so $H$ contains an interval and is therefore dense. Being the preimage of $\{0\}$ under continuous $g$ (if $g$ were continuous) — but actually $H$ is measurable, which suffices.

title: Wild Additive Functions Exist (AC)
content:
**Axiom** (`wild_additive_exist`): There exist additive functions that are discontinuous everywhere.

Using the Axiom of Choice, fix a Hamel basis $B$ for $\mathbb{R}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Define $f$ to be 1 on one basis element and 0 on all others, then extend $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly. This $f$ is additive but discontinuous, non-measurable, and its graph is dense in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

Hamel (1905) first constructed such functions. Their existence depends on AC; in Solovay's model, every set is Lebesgue measurable and every additive function is linear.
mathContext: A Hamel basis $B$ has $|B| = |\mathbb{R}| = 2^{\aleph_0}$. Any function $\phi: B \to \mathbb{R}$ extends uniquely to an additive $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$. If $\phi$ is not the restriction of a linear function, then $f$ is wild.

title: Measurable Additive Functions are Linear
content:
**Axiom** (`measurable_additive_is_linear`): If $f$ is additive and Lebesgue measurable, then $f(x) = cx$ for some $c$.

This strengthens Cauchy's theorem: measurability suffices instead of continuity. In fact, even weaker conditions work: boundedness on a set of positive measure (Ostrowski, 1929), or Baire measurability, or local boundedness at a single point.

The proof uses Steinhaus/Lusin: if $f$ is measurable, then $f$ is approximately continuous a.e., which forces the standard $f(q) = qf(1)$ argument to extend from $\mathbb{Q}$ to $\mathbb{R}$.
mathContext: Ostrowski's theorem (1929): If $f$ is additive and bounded above on a set of positive measure (or on an interval), then $f(x) = f(1) \cdot x$. Measurability $\Rightarrow$ Lusin's theorem $\Rightarrow$ approximate continuity $\Rightarrow$ local boundedness $\Rightarrow$ linearity.

title: Summary Theorem: Main Result + Uniqueness
content:
**Theorem** (`erdos_1126_summary`): Combines the de Bruijn-Jurkat theorem with uniqueness into a single statement:

1. $\forall f,\, \text{IsAlmostAdditive}(f) \Rightarrow \exists g,\, \text{IsAdditive}(g) \wedge f =_{\text{a.e.}} g$
2. $\forall g_1\, g_2,\, \text{IsAdditive}(g_1) \wedge \text{IsAdditive}(g_2) \wedge g_1 =_{\text{a.e.}} g_2 \Rightarrow g_1 = g_2$

Proved by pairing `de_bruijn_jurkat_theorem` and `additive_ae_unique` as `⟨..., ...⟩`.

This is the complete answer to Erdős Problem #1126: **SOLVED**.
mathContext: Together, (1) and (2) show that the map $\text{Additive} \to \text{AlmostAdditive}/\sim_{\text{a.e.}}$ is a bijection. Every a.e. equivalence class of almost-additive functions contains exactly one additive function.
